questions.text:
Consider a single processor system with four processes A, B, C, and D, represented as given below, where for each process the first value is its arrival time, and the second value is its CPU burst time.

A (0, 10), B (2, 6), C (4, 3), and D (6, 7).

Which one of the following options gives the average waiting times when preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) and Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (NP-SJF) CPU scheduling algorithms are applied to the processes?
questions.solution:
SRTF Gantt chart: A(0-2), B(2-4), C(4-7), B(7-11), D(11-18), A(18-26)
Waiting = completion [latex]-[/latex] arrival [latex]-[/latex] burst:
A = 26[latex]-[/latex]0[latex]-[/latex]10 = 16, B = 11[latex]-[/latex]2[latex]-[/latex]6 = 3, C = 7[latex]-[/latex]4[latex]-[/latex]3 = 0, D = 18[latex]-[/latex]6[latex]-[/latex]7 = 5
Average [latex]=24/4=6[/latex]

NP-SJF Gantt chart: A(0-10), C(10-13), B(13-19), D(19-26)
Waiting: A = 0, C = 10[latex]-[/latex]4 = 6, B = 13[latex]-[/latex]2 = 11, D = 19[latex]-[/latex]6 = 13
Average [latex]=30/4=7.5[/latex]

Answer: SRTF = 6, NP-SJF = 7.5

questions.text: Consider a process P running on a CPU. Which one or more of the following events will always trigger a context switch by the OS that results in process P moving to a non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Blocking system call to read disk: P must wait for I/O [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] moved to blocked state [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Page fault for a page in swap space: the page must be read from disk [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is blocked [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Disk interrupt for another process: the OS handles it and makes that process ready, but P can continue running [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.
- Timer interrupt: P may still have time left in its slice, or the scheduler may pick P again [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: P makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
P tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware

questions.text:
Which of the following tasks is/are the responsibility/responsibilities of the memory
management unit (MMU) in a system with paging-based memory management?
questions.solution:
The MMU is hardware that sits between CPU and memory. Its jobs:
- Translate virtual address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] physical address using the page table True
- Raise a trap (page fault) when the entry is invalid / not present True
- Raise a trap when a write is attempted on a read-only page True

Allocating a page table for a new process is done by the OS (software), not the MMU.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Allocate a new page table for a newly created process
Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table
Raise a trap when a virtual address is not found in the page table
Raise a trap when a process tries to write to a page marked with read-only permission in the page table

questions.text: Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of [latex] 2 \mathrm{~KB} [/latex]. Assume that both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages [latex] 0,1,2 [/latex], and [latex]3[/latex] are stored in the page frames [latex] 1,3,2 [/latex], and [latex]0[/latex], respectively. The physical address (in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address [latex]2500[/latex] (in decimal format) is ____
questions.solution:
Page size [latex]=2\text{ KB}=2048[/latex].

[latex]2500=1\times2048+452[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] page 1, offset 452.
Page 1 is in frame 3.

Physical address [latex]=3\times2048+452=6144+452=6596[/latex]

Answer: 6596

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

In each iteration every existing process calls fork(), so the number of processes doubles, and each of them prints once. (wait() only changes the order, not the count; each child continues the loop with the current x.)

- x = 3: 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 processes, prints 2
- x = 2: 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 processes, prints 4
- x = 1: 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 processes, prints 8

Total [latex]=2+4+8=14[/latex]

Answer: 14
